opus-5.5.text:
I think it's really a two-way thing, and honestly I've learned at least as much from my students as from my own teachers.

When I was a student, what mattered most from my advisors and mentors wasn't any particular technique. It was taste: what problems are worth working on, what counts as a clean idea versus a hack, when to keep pushing and when to drop something. You absorb that by watching how someone reacts to a result. Do they get excited about a simple idea that works, or only about a big number on a benchmark? That shapes you for a long time, often without your noticing.

Now that I have students, the direction flips in an interesting way. Students come in without the baggage I carry. They don't know that something "isn't supposed to work," so they try it, and sometimes it does work. That's very humbling. A lot of what I believe about research has been revised because a student came back with a result I didn't expect, or asked a naive question I couldn't answer well. In a field moving as fast as AI, my intuitions from five years ago can quickly become a liability, and students are often the ones who pull me out of that.

So I see my role less as transferring knowledge and more as protecting the conditions for good thinking: giving people room to explore, being honest about what I think is interesting, and then being willing to be proven wrong. The best moments are when a student ends up with a taste that's different from mine, and better. That's the point. Research is a kind of lineage. Ideas and values get passed along, but each generation should mutate them a little.

r001.rationale: The response says the speaker has learned at least as much from students as from teachers, and describes students revising his research beliefs.

r002.rationale: It presents influence as reciprocal across generations: teachers shape the speaker, students shape him in turn, and ideas and values pass along a lineage and mutate.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because I've been on both sides of it.

When I was a student, I was very lucky with my advisors. The thing they gave me wasn't really technical knowledge. You can get that from papers. What they gave me was taste. A sense for which problems are worth working on, and which ones are just fashionable. I remember being pushed to ask, over and over, "What is the simplest version of this idea?" That instinct toward simplicity, toward removing things rather than adding them, came straight from the people I trained under. A lot of my later work, like ConvNeXt, is really just that lesson applied again and again.

The other thing teachers do is give you permission. Research is full of moments where the obvious move is to follow the crowd, and a good advisor says, "No, trust your own observation, go check it." That changes you. It makes you willing to look at something everyone has accepted and say, maybe this isn't right.

Now that I'm a professor, I've realized students shape me at least as much. They come in without the baggage. They haven't absorbed the field's assumptions yet, so they ask questions that an expert would never ask, and sometimes those questions are exactly the right ones. I'll have a mental model of why something works, a student will poke at it, and I'll discover I never actually had evidence for it. That happens more often than I'd like to admit.

Students also keep you honest about time. I'm busy, I'm distracted, and they're the ones in the lab running the experiments and seeing the surprising failure case at two in the morning. If I don't listen carefully, I miss the most important signal in the whole project.

So I think of it less as teaching and more as a kind of long conversation. You pass along taste and courage to your students, and they pass back fresh eyes and data you'd otherwise never see. The best moments in my career have come when both directions were working at once.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says students shape their professors, providing fresh questions, challenges, and experimental evidence.

r002.rationale: It describes advisors and students as part of a reciprocal exchange: teachers pass along taste and courage, while students return fresh perspectives and data.

astra-6.text:
I think students and teachers shape your thinking in different but complementary ways. A teacher gives you a sense of what matters: how to choose a problem, how to ask a precise question, and how to recognize when you haven’t really understood something. Often, that way of thinking stays with you longer than any particular piece of knowledge.

Students push you to examine those habits. They ask why something has to be done a certain way, and sometimes you realize your answer is just, “That’s how I learned it.” Explaining an idea to them forces you to clarify it for yourself. And their questions can reveal possibilities you’ve stopped considering.

So I see it as a continuous exchange. You learn from your teachers how to approach the world, and your students help you keep that approach open to change.

r001.rationale: The response says students’ questions challenge teachers’ habits, clarify ideas, and help keep their thinking open to change.

r002.rationale: It describes teachers and students as connected through a continuous, reciprocal exchange that shapes how each approaches the world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think students and teachers shape your thinking in different ways. A teacher can help you recognize what matters—how to choose a problem, how to question an assumption, how to keep going when something doesn’t work. Often, what stays with you is their way of thinking rather than a particular answer.

Students push you from the other direction. They ask questions about things you’ve started to take for granted. When you try to explain an idea to them, you sometimes discover that your own understanding isn’t as clear as you thought. And they bring their own perspectives, so the conversation can take you somewhere you wouldn’t have gone alone.

So I see it as a continuous exchange. You learn from your teachers, but being a teacher also changes how you learn.

r001.rationale: The response says students challenge taken-for-granted ideas and expose gaps in teachers’ understanding, conveying that teachers learn from students.

r002.rationale: It describes reciprocal learning between teachers and students, but does not frame the people who shape cognition as an interconnected network.
